subtopic: ALLEGED LACK OF CONSULTATION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I gave the Chair notice that I wanted to raise, at the first opportunity, a question of privilege on the manner in which the government proceeded yesterday, and I am referring to the fact that the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs) gave notice pursuant to Standing Order 78(3). I would like to read the following which appears at page 2095 of the Votes and Proceedings for Wednesday, October 10, 1990:
Mr. McDermid, a Member of the Queen's Privy Council, from his place in the House, stated that an agreement could not be reached under the provisions of Standing Orders 78(1) and 78(2) with respect to an allocation of time to the second reading stage of Bill C-84, An Act respecting the privatization of the national petroleum company of Canada, and, under the provisions of Standing Order 78(3), gave notice of his intention to move a motion at the next sitting of the House for the purpose of allotting a specified number of days, or a day, for the consideration and disposal of that stage of the said Bill,
Mr. Speaker, this happened late yesterday, after we had heard three speakers in a debate that started yesterday in the House-three speakers on a very important bill.
Mr. Speaker, I will try to be as brief as possible. The notice given by the minister is irregular, because he misled the House by implying that Standing Orders 78(1) and 78(2) had been used. Not so, Mr. Speaker! Neither 78(1) nor 78(2) were used, and as for 78(3), according to us, according to the traditions and customs of this House, in fact for more than 20 years, Mr. Speaker, since 1969, when the Standing Orders were amended, the government has always been required to make every effort to
consult with the party of the government's Official Opposition-in this case the Liberal Party-and the other parties in this House, in this case the New Democratic Party.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that neither the Parliamentary House Leader of the Liberal Party nor the Deputy House Leader and Whip, the hon. member for Cape Breton-Richmond East, nor my colleague, friend and deputy, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, nor the Deputy Whip of the Official Opposition, the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, Mr. Boudria, were ever consulted.
Therefore, no one in this House can say there has been any attempt to consult with the Official Opposition pursuant to Standing Orders 78(1) and 78(2). Mr. Speaker, what do these Standing Orders say? I will read them, because this is very important.

78.(1) When a Minister of the Crown, from his or her place in the House, states that there is agreement among the representatives of all parties to allot a specified number of days or hours to the proceedings at one or more stages of any public bill, the Minister may propose a motion, without notice, setting forth the terms of such agreed allocation; and every such motion shall be decided forthwith, without debate or amendment.
Mr. Speaker, that has not been done. That was not done by the government.
Standing Order 78(2), Mr. Speaker, which flows after Standing Order 78(1), reads as follows:
(2) When a Minister of the Crown, from his or her place in the House, states that a majority of the representatives of the several parties have come to an agreement -
And I underline "several parties have come to an agreement":
- in respect of a proposed allotment of days or hours for the proceedings at any stage of the passing of a public bill, the Minister may propose a motion, without notice, during proceedings under Government Orders, setting forth the terms of the said proposed allocation; provided that for the purposes of this section of this Standing Order an allocation may be proposed in one motion to cover the proceedings at both the report and the third reading stages of a bill if that motion is consistent with the provisions of Standing Order 76(10). During the consideration of any such motion no Member may speak more than once or longer than ten minutes. Not more than two hours after the commencement of proceedings

thereon, the Speaker shall put every question necessary to dispose of the said motion. Any proceeding interrupted pursuant to this section of this Standing Order shall be deemed adjourned.
Mr. Speaker, that was not done. Standing Order 78(2) was not followed. From all this flows Standing Order 78(3) which says that if we could not get agreement under Standing Order 78(1) and we could not get agreement under Standing Order 78(2), then the government can come and consult with the parties and possibly after that consultation give a notice. I will read it:
(3) A Minister of the Crown who from his or her place in the House, at a previous sitting, has stated that an agreement could not be reached under the provisions of sections (1) or (2) of this Standing Order in respect of proceedings at the stage at which a public bill was then under consideration either in the House or in any committee, and has given notice of his or her intention so to do, may propose a motion during proceedings under Government Orders, for the purpose of allotting a specified number of days or hours for the consideration and disposal of proceedings at that stage; provided that the time allotted for any stage is not to be less than one sitting day and provided that for the purposes of this section of this Standing Order an allocation may be proposed in one motion to cover the proceedings at both the report and the third reading stages on a bill -
And so on. Mr. Speaker, yesterday, I submit to you, this House was misled intentionally by this government, was not-

The minister yesterday said there has been no agreement. How the heck could he say that when he knows darn well that there was no consultation with anybody on this side of the House? How could the minister, in his great intelligence, decide that the opposition, after three speakers in the House, had been consulted because he heard from this side opposition views on that bill? What does that mean, Mr. Speaker?
I have been around here for 18 years and a lot of people in this House believed and thought that the customs, the procedures, and the usual way of doing things, the courteous thing, was to have consultations under Standing Order 78(1). That is the practice in the House, for those who are listening.
The rule says that the government comes to the opposition and says: "We would like to limit the debate on such and such a measure, or such a bill or motion. Would you agree to give us debate for maybe two or three days?" That has been done over the years since 1969. As I said before, that has been the practice. That has been the custom. That has been the rule of the House.
If the government could not get agreement under Standing Order 78(1) from all parties, maybe a majority
of the parties, maybe two of the three parties in the House, would agree. That was Standing Order 78(2). If not, then it could use Standing Order 78(3) and give notice that no agreement could be reached. My argument to you, Mr. Speaker, is that by saying to Canadians and to the House that Standing Orders 78(1) and 78(2), as we used them, is false. The government never used Standing Order 78(1). Mr. Speaker, the point I want to make is that in fact what has happened is time allocation and closure. These are the rules which are provided for our use in this House. They have become part of our operating system and have been used for more than 10 years. It is interesting that today it balances out, 26 times in the previous four years prior to 1984, and six times since.
It is interesting to read Standing Orders 78.(1), (2) and (3). I would like to refer to phrases in them. In Standing Order 78.(1) it states there is an agreement. In 78.(2) it states that the majority of the representatives of the several parties have come to an agreement. However, Standing Order 78.(3) says in the third line that an agreement could not be reached under the provisions of the previous sections.
What is interesting about that particular wording is that it mentions an agreement but it does not mention the process. That is very crucial here. It is very central to the issue we are discussing at the moment. The reason it is so crucial is that it does not say or lay out a process that has to be followed with a little check list, and at the end of that check list one says the check list is completed, therefore this action takes place.
There is a very important reason, I believe, why the drafters of the Standing Order chose that particular wording. Essentially, what we are up against is that in order to have an agreement, you have to have a conversation. You have to have a discussion. However, there have been times, and it is not only today, but at other times in the past, that it is impossible to have that conversation. Therefore, just because that particular conversation does not take place does not mean that there have not been attempts for consultation and that the requirements of Standing Order 78.(1) and (2) have not been fulfilled.

Yesterday the hon. member who rose on the point of order, the House leader for the Official Opposition was doing some important work in committee. I know that. As a result of that, yesterday I attempted to talk to the Whip of the Liberal Party. I attempted on three different occasions to talk to him. He was in and out of the House so we kept missing one another. I left word in the back room that I wished to speak to him. The reason I point this out is that there were attempts on my part to have a discussion with the Official Opposition to go through this process. While going through the process of trying to have my discussions yesterday, I ended up talking with the House leader for the NDP. During the conversations we had it became
very obvious to me that in fact there was no possibility for agreement under Standing Order 78(1). That one was clearly ruled out.
I attempted then to have conversations with the Official Opposition but was not successful. Mr. Speaker, we could not reach an agreement. We have offered on several occasions, including as much as an hour and a half ago, to have further consultations to come to some sort of agreement. That was refused and obviously we do not have an agreement.
I think, Mr. Speaker, the notice of motion that was given yesterday by the minister was a perfectly legitimate motion. It was obvious that there was not agreement, and there was every reason to believe, as has been confirmed, that there was no agreement.

So although my friend makes a very persuasive argument, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that it simply is not a legitimate point of privilege. Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my friend the parliamentary secretary and while I find his comments to be interesting I do not find them terribly relevant.
I want to say right from the beginning that this is a most serious issue which the House leader for the Official Opposition has raised. The rules are there to be followed precisely and I would suggest that they were written with care. Any of us who have gone through the process of attempting to write standing orders recognizes the care and thought that goes into the wording of a particular standing order.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to some precedents first of all. I want to go back to April 14, 1987, during the debate on Bill C-22, when the Speaker at that point made this comment:
Rules of procedure-are designed to allow the full expression of views on both sides of an issue. They provide the Opposition with a means to delay a decision. They also provide the majority with a means of limiting debate in order to arrive at a decision. This is the kind of balance essential to the procedure of a democratic assembly. Our rules were certainly never designed to permit the total frustration of one side or the other-
Mr. Speaker, I also refer to the February 7, 1990 Hansard at page 7948 when you made the following comments:
Notice of time allocation motions after only a few hours of debate at any stage of a Bill can also be an abuse.
First of all to put this into some context, and I think the record is very clear, the Conservatives have in their six years doubled the use of closure and time allocation in the whole history of Parliament since 1867. In other words, no other government has used closure and time allocation to the extent of this particular government in our entire history. We have seen in committees, in this House, as well as the other place, an abuse of the rules, tradition, custom, interpretation and convention.
My recollection is that at the most recent House leaders meeting, which took place on Tuesday afternoon, I do not recall at that time whether there was a discussion as to the limits of debate on the privatization of Petro-Canada. I do not recall that. I do, however, agree with my hon. friend, the parliamentary secretary,

speechtext:
The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier rose earlier this morning on a question of privilege concerning whether or not the hon. minister had given valid notice pursuant to the provisions of sections 78(1), 78(2) and 78(3) of the Standing Orders relating to time allocation.
The hon. minister said "I am informed that to date agreement has not been reached under the provisions," et cetera. I point out that he also said "we will try to get an agreement with the opposition parties on a reasonable length of time".
There has been considerable discussion this morning with respect to what is or what is not required under the Standing Order in terms of consultation or exchange of views between the government and others in the Chamber.
I want it clearly understood that my ruling today does not turn in any way, or on any particular, on any of the comments that were made during arguments as to the question of discussions between, or lack of discussions between, anybody in this Chamber at all.
My ruling does not take anything away from rulings of past Speakers, and especially my ruling of some months ago, in March I think of last year. It made it very clear that under the rules it is not for the Speaker to go behind the statement of the minister and try to make a factual ruling as to whether or not discussions were adequate or inadequate or, for that matter, try to strain the rules and to try to give an interpretation that substitutes for the plain wording of the rule.
I have also indicated that it might be in the interests of the House that the entire rule was looked at again, reconsidered, and perhaps redrafted.
The rule I am bound by, and this place lives by the rule of law, is the plain words of Ruling 78.(3) and it states:
A Minister of the Crown who from his or her place in the House,
at a previous sitting, has stated that an agreement could not be
reached under the provisions of-

In English:
(3) A Minister of the Crown who from his or her place in the House, at a previous sitting, has stated an agreement could not be reached -

It sometimes happens that when one has to try to interpret what is meant by words, some guidance or some difference shows up between the English and the French. There is, in my opinion, absolutely no difference whatsoever in the meaning of those words either in English or in French.
As I have pointed out, the hon. minister said: "I have been informed to date that agreement has not been reached." I find on this very narrow ground, but one which I cannot ignore as your Speaker because it is clearly there in the rules, that the minister should have said "could not be reached." That is what is required under the ruling and, as a consequence, I have to rule that the notice given yesterday is not valid. Of course, it is for the government to decide whether it wishes to give the notice again.

To the retailers I had the privilege to represent during the past 20 years, I want to say that Petro-Canada was a real problem for us. Mr. Speaker, Red Deer said goodbye to one of its best this week with the passing of former mayor Ed Barrett. I was privileged to join a packed congregation to celebrate the life of a well loved and respected community leader.
Mr. Barrett gave a lifetime of service to his community. He served 13 years on city council. He was mayor from 1965 to 1974. He was president of the Alberta Urban Municipalities Association, and very active in his church, especially the choir, where he was known for his fine singing voice.
He retired in 1974 and was named Red Deer's Citizen of the Year. But Ed Barrett did not stop there. He became very active in organizing seniors' groups and was still heard singing in the hospital last week.
Ed Barrett will be remembered for many things, most importantly for his honesty and integrity. He was an example for everyone who was privileged to know him.

Mr. Speaker, it has been deeply disappointing and frustrating to most Canadians, and certainly to me, that some of our citizens, particularly in Quebec but also among our native Indian bands, seek a separate sovereignty, apart from Canada. I cannot and will not support any directions that promote a separate Canada.
The unity of this country is our most compelling priority. However, this is not to say that we should try to prevent anyone from exercising his or her freedom to feel or to think or to speak differently in Canada, even though it may be for extreme positions such as separation. Our democracy is surely strong enough for that. It will stand the test of dissent and division. In fact, it will be that very spirit of free democracy that will ultimately keep us together.
For example, as much as I oppose the separation of Quebec, which is the cause that motivates some of our independent members from Quebec, and as strongly as I will work to defend Canadian unity against their efforts, nevertheless I do support their elected right to represent their constituents as they see fit.
We shall not be able to demonstrate the virtues of Canadianism by obstructing or squelching free thought or free speech. Rather, we will establish those virtues by tolerating dissent and debate and by defeating wrong directions in democratic ways.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance who was warned last spring by western premiers about a made-in-Canada recession. They used that term, made-in-Cana-da recession. They warned him about the use of high interest rates, the lack of confidence in his policies and the imposition of the GST, which would only worsen the condition of the western economy.

In the face of 268 farm bankruptcies on the prairies, the loss of 11,000 manufacturing jobs in Manitoba alone, will the minister now admit that he and his policies are a total and dreadful failure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is selectively referring to what the premiers said. He neglects to say that in 1988 they unanimously came out with a recommendation to get interest rates down. If we had done that, we would have a rip-roaring inflation problem today, the likes of which they have in the United Kingdom today. I remind hon. members that the inflation rate in the United Kingdom is 10.6 per cent.
The hon. member criticizes the GST, saying that it will be tough on agriculture. What my hon. friend should do is go and speak to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. They will explain to him that they support the GST because there will be a $250 million saving to agriculture. Let me repeat that, Mr. Speaker, a $250 million saving for agriculture as a result of the elimination of the federal sales tax and the introduction of the goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, I wish this minister would come west. My home city of Winnipeg has a proud heritage in transportation, yet this week there were 223 more lay-offs at Air Canada and 125 more lost jobs at CN Rail, which will result in taking $8 million out of the Winnipeg economy. I have said nothing about the total collapse of the trucking industry in my province.
I want to ask the Minister this. Will he now realize that Manitobans are hurting, as are all Canadians, and that his policies are crippling the Manitoba economy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have never said that Canadians are not hurting. I understand-
You said it was silly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No, no, I said the Leader of the Opposition was silly.
I have said that I understand that the period we are going through now, which I anticipated some while ago, would be a difficult one for Canadians. But what we have to understand is the alternatives.
Oral Questions
We could have avoided this period we are going through now. We could have let the party go on for another three, six, or nine months, but then the problems would be that much greater. What we are trying to do is avoid the boom and the bust that we had in 1981-82 by taking steps earlier to anticipate the problem and to get the problem under control before we lose control of it, and that is precisely what we are going through now.
I said in my budget that there will be great demands for quick-fix solutions to this, quick-fix solutions that are not possible. Unfortunately, my colleague is looking for a quick-fix solution which simply will not work.

Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic provinces are in agony. Prohibitive interest rates, hundreds of jobs gone, yesterday, at Air Canada and its Atlantic service division, the looming GST, and now a man-made recession. I have a question for the man, the Minister of Finance.
Why is he hell-bent on destroying the Atlantic provinces and why does he consider their fears about this situation, in his own words, silly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is silly for the hon. member to suggest that I am hell-bent on destroying the economy of the Atlantic provinces. What I have tried to explain to the hon. member and her colleagues is the basis for the policy that we have been following.
She should reflect back to what happened in the 1970s and the early 1980s. The government of the day swept the problem of inflation under the carpet and allowed inflation to go to 13 per cent. That resulted in interest rates of 20 per cent to 25 per cent and that, Mr. Speaker, did destroy the economy of Atlantic Canada. If she could understand the fact that we tried to anticipate the problem in this business cycle, not let inflation get out of control, and avoid the problems that we ran into in the 1970s and early 1980s, she would understand the basis for the policy that we are following today. It is a policy of leadership, of avoiding problems before they get out of control.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. minister avoids any more problems, the Atlantic provinces will disappear. Overnight, in Nova Scotia, heating oil is up three cents a litre, gas is up two cents a litre, and the other Atlantic provinces will soon have to follow suit. In our region, this winter, Canadians will be unemployed

and they will be freezing in the dark. Will the minister, for the love of God, change his policy?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you left the Chair, you said I had ten minutes left. I will now continue my speech on the privatization of Petro-Cana-da.
As I said this morning, I have tried to explain why Petro-Canada has been of no use to either retailers or consumers. I tried to find some benefits, and found not a single one. Petro-Canada was a failure. There was nothing in it for Canadians.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: That's true!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
First of all, the government has no business selling gas, Mr. Speaker, any more than it does selling tooth brushes. It is absolutely ridiculous to use taxpayers' money to take over a company in the private sector, considering the private sector was in perfectly good shape.
This party feels that private sector deserves our confidence. Today, Mr. Speaker, I thought again during lunch about the fact that Petro-Canada never played the leading role it was supposed to play. Petro-Canada was always a bone of contention. Let me give you an example. When Petro-Canada sold gas for one cent a litre less than private companies like Esso, for instance, the next day, everybody called the government to complain that Petro-Canada was cutting its prices. Whenever Petro-Canada decided to charge one cent more, the next day Canadian consumers would be on the phone, saying: This is our company, so why do we have to pay more? It doesn't make sense. That is what we had to contend with for six years, when we got those calls in our ridings.
As a company, Petro-Canada was in a conflict-of-interest situation from the outset because it was powerless.
Government Orders
It was always an extension of the government and only did what the government told it to do.
Petro-Canada's slogan was something like: "It belongs to us". Mr. Speaker, I have given this a lot of thought over the years, and I think I have the answer. It doesn't belong to us, because nobody can go there and get free or cheaper gas. Several times it reminded me of the time when Shell had a slogan: Shell helps those who help themselves. The Shell retailers I represented said: Help yourself, because Shell certainly won't. Petro-Canada belongs to you. Maybe they left out something and it should read: Petro-Canada does not belong to you. Maybe that's what they meant. Although the Liberals said at the time it was a window opening on the industry, I didn't see a very big window and I didn't see what consumers stood to gain either.
Mr. Speaker, Petro-Canada will have a fantastic future thanks to privatization. With or without a war in Kuwait, according to the experts and analysts the next five years will be excellent for the oil industry, and that includes Petro-Canada.
Members opposite who like Petro-Canada and who still object to the bill-only yesterday, we had one member who said he was going to vote against the bill. The hon. member for York Centre, from the Toronto area, said that the opposition was not in favour of privatizing Petro-Canada. He has forgotten that oil companies are promised a bright future, whether or not there is a war in Kuwait. They are going through difficult times just now. The Opposition just cannot admit that Petro-Canada should not be a Crown corporation.
Petro-Canada has not discovered a single barrel of oil, not even a glass. It was supposed to show leadership and assume the duties of existing organizations. Not a barrel, not even a cup. Yet, the people opposite want to keep it. On a diet for the past year, Petro-Canada has dropped a lot of deadweight. It has sold 1,200 of its service stations. From now on, therefore, this company will be able to do its job like the others, on the same level as the others, and will be able likewise to get financing. The good thing about that Petro-Canada will no longer be a political tool in the hands of a minister such as Mr. Lalonde who could call and say: On such and such a day, you are going to do this, you are going to do that.

October 11, 1990
Government Orders
That era is over! We must let private enterprise operate without government interference. Why is the government not selling tooth brushes? I wonder why. What did the retailers get? At first, when they received their Petro-Canada signs, they were happy because they were part of a big organization and expected to make millions. They were even forbidden to hang on the wall pictures of their families. They would work like slaves from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. because their manager in his ivory tower in Calgary had said that those were the opening hours. When retailers complained that not a single customer would show up after 9 p.m, they were told that it did not matter, that Petro-Canada stations remained open until 11 p.m., and that was that! Do you call that living? I know a number of retailers who ruined their personnel lives, their family lives, received hardly any salaries and got no return on their investments. They lost everything because Petro-canada, a Crown corporation, was forcing them to remain open until 11 p.m. Petro-Canada wanted to keep a nice profile, because the minister used to call it once in a while; it had to look good politically, especially once every four years, come election time. That is what Petro-Canada did for our people.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my colleagues who, with me, formed a team in 1985 to suggest this privatization to the government. I wish to thank also all the ministers, their advisers and especially our Prime Minister who listened to us and other Canadians, because in my own riding of Laval, in Quebec, I have not met many people who are great supporters of Petro-Canada. Each time there was a price increase, Petro-Canada, which was supposed to monitor the industry, just went along. When there were decreases, it went along too. But it never led the way. It just followed; they were a bunch of "followers".
Today, Mr. Speaker, I am proud to tell my constituents who are listening to me that I did keep the promise I made in 1984 and repeated in 1988, that Petro-Canada would be privatized and that the National Energy Program would be abolished. Today, Mr. Speaker, I can tell them "mission accomplished!". And it is a mission accomplished for a number of Quebec ridings. I toured Quebec and visited quite a few service station operators, I knew 7,000 of them when I was their representative. All
the way from Montreal to Gaspe, and along the Ontario border as well. The agents who wore the Petro-Canada cap certainly did not have it made, quite the contrary, they had to work harder and for lower returns than others operating in the private sector.
I had the pleasure of working 14 years with Imperial Oil. These turned out to be the 14 most disastrous years of my life because Imperial Oil management were heartless. I do not know if they have mellowed since, but I rather doubt it. Their one and only concern was the dollar. When private sector dealers are battling it out on a level field, fair is fair, but when war is being waged with Canadian taxpayers' money I can tell you that you may be hard pressed to stand the competition.
As I said in my remarks this morning, each private station service operator had an annual budget of $1,000 for sprucing up the place, while each Petro-Canada agent could spend as much as $50,000 for the same thing. They would even break up the concrete to clean up although it was not necessary. It did not matter, they were spending taxpayers' money. The Liberals are second to none when it comes to spending money. Goodbye, thank you, not to worry! Marc Lalonde, a nice picture I have kept since 1981, Canada's No. 1 gas jockey, "Marc Lalonde, October 24, 1981". See what he looks like! subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in listening to the hon. member for Burin-St. George's.
It is always nice to know that there are other common people in this House. I guess that is not improper since this is the House of Commons.
The hon. member is a carpenter's son who found his way here. I am a poor rancher's boy who found his way into the Chilcotin plateau. I, too, am struggling to understand the complexities of this major bill for us.
Earlier, the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs) laid out in clear and simple language the reason for this government proposal. Today, I would like to discuss how this proposed transaction fits into the
Government Orders
broader approach to privatization which has been followed by the government since 1984.
When the current government was elected in 1984, one of its first priorities was to restructure the country's economic framework to enable Canadians to become more competitive to meet the challenging of the emerging global marketplace.
In the past six years, this government has pursued an economic policy based on less government involvement in the private sector, a more disciplined use of the taxpayers' resources. Privatization, I am glad to say, is a key component of that policy. As many of you know, in the last half of the last decade governments of every political persuasion started to critically examine the old solutions to see if they had utility in a modem world of global competition. Not only did they find that the old practices of central planning and excessive intervention by governments were ineffective, they were counter-productive. They impaired the nation's ability to compete.
In the struggle to transform the economies of many of the democracies of eastern Europe in particular, governments there are embracing the notion of privatization in different ways and in varying degrees. While Canada is providing assistance to several of these countries in implementing their privatization programs, we cannot forget that we still have a lot of work to do in our own backyard.
At last count the Canadian government owned 53 Crown corporations and 113 subsidiary Crown corporations and had partial holdings in a number of other firms. This is after having successfully privatized 13 Crown corporations and Crown holdings in five mixed ownership corporations. Some of these include Canadair, an aircraft manufacturer; Teleglobe Canada, our overseas telecommunications carrier; and of course Air Canada, Canada's largest airline which was sold through two public share offerings to over 100,000 shareholders.
The success of Canada's approach to privatization is due largely to the fact that it reflects, and attempts to reflect the country's unique demographic, economic, political, and historical considerations. Consider for a moment the disparity between our geography and our population. Canada is the largest country in the western hemisphere. Compared to the U.S. with only 3.6 million square miles, Canada has 3.8. On the other hand we have a population of only 26 million, a tenth of that of the United States.

October 11, 1990
Government Orders
This disparity between our geography and our population has encouraged a reliance on government ownership as a way of supplying vital national services such as rail and air transport. Some of the customers of these services express concern that a change in ownership will mean a reduction in service or safety, or increased prices. Therefore, in developing its privatization plans the government gives special consideration to the concerns of these customers. Where necessary, regulations are introduced to ensure that health and safety standards are maintained.
Another factor explaining Canada's approach to privatization is the role of foreign ownership in our economy. Canada's economic development gave rise to the industrial base dominated by branch plants. Most of Canada's manufacturing and petroleum product sectors are still dominated by subsidiaries of companies headquartered outside of Canada.
As a result, Canadians have welcomed the financial benefits of foreign investment while remaining a bit nervous about the consequences of foreign influence on our economy. Because of this, the government's privatization program looks at the foreign ownership question on a case-by-case basis to determine whether non-resident restrictions are indeed required.
Canada's privatization program is also influenced by our Constitution, in particular its division of powers between federal and provincial governments. Canada's Constitution gives the provinces control over the regulation of the securities industry. The provincial securities commissions each impose constraints on what can be done to promote a public share offering. In these instances where a public share offering is used as a method of sale, this regulatory environment must be taken into account.
One final factor which contributes to the uniqueness of our privatization policy is the character and condition of Canadians themselves. Canadians are highly educated, participate actively in a free enterprise economy, and enjoy a high standard of living compared to other countries. Most Canadians own their own houses. Many of them own shares as well.
Canada did not have to promote "popular capitalism" as part of its privatization program because it was already a reality in the Canadian culture.
In fact more than four million Canadians or 23 per cent of the Canadian adult population own shares in a publicly traded company or in as stock mutual fund. This represents an increase of about one million share owners since 1986, when 18 per cent of Canadian adults participated in the stock market.
All these uniquely Canadian circumstances-a small population in a large land mass, the predominance of branch plants, our Constitution with its complex division of powers between the provincial and federal governments, and the nature of our domestic capital markets- had to be taken into account when the government first got itself into the business of owning commercial interests. They must be taken into account now as we get out of some of them.
The minister has assured us that the government's privatization program is based on a pragmatic, common sense, case by case approach. The time is taken to examine very carefully the circumstances associated with each company in order to determine the best method and timing of the sale.
It may be useful to look back on some of the major privatizations which have taken place since 1984 to show the pragmatic and intelligent approach that has been taken. In my opinion three transactions stand out: the sale of Canadair to Bombardier, the sale of Teleglobe to Memotec Data, and the privatization of Air Canada. I would like to take each one in turn.
First is the sale of Canadair. Canadians know that the sale of Canadair to Bombardier has been a tremendous success story. They know that Canadair was going nowhere under state ownership. It was a company with excellent technology but poor marketing and poor management skills. Those are exactly the ingredients which Bombardier brought to the enterprise. There is simply no question that the privatization of Canadair has given the company a bright and exciting future.
Second is Teleglobe. The Teleglobe case in an excellent example. You do not have to own a company to control it. In this case the price of overseas telephone calls can easily be controlled through regulation if that is desired. What was accomplished by relying on regula-

Government Orders
tion, not ownership, was the creation of a dynamic new force in the Canadian telecommunications sector, Me-motec Data. Once again it was a win win situation.
Third is Air Canada. Crown ownership of Air Canada may have been necessary in earlier days to achieve the public policy objective of creating a national air system, but we all know that circumstances have radically changed in air transportation since those early days. Now we have two major airlines in Canada with myriad commuter lines servicing smaller centres. We now have a national air system with many participants. In short, public ownership of Air Canada was no longer essential to ensure a national air service.
Furthermore, Air Canada required a large infusion of capital to finance fleet modernization. We therefore had the choice of raising that money through higher taxes or higher deficit, or raising money through public share offerings. Since Crown ownership was no longer necessary, we chose to offer shares to the public which were well received by Air Canada employees and the general public alike.
These transactions are not the product of ideology. In my view, they represent the triumph of common sense over the impassioned rhetoric of the proponents of state ownership. They have set the stage for the government's latest privatization initiative: the sale of Petro-Canada.
As the minister stated earlier, Crown ownership is no longer necessary to achieve the principal public policy objective in the energy sector to establish the conditions in which economic development of our energy reserves can occur.
What is necessary for Petro-Canada to participate aggressively in the development of our oil and gas reserves is access to a new and reliable source of equity. Once again, we are left with a choice in the House of finding that money by taxing Canadians, by borrowing even more money on their behalf, or by inviting Canadians to take a direct stake in the company to share the challenge which lies ahead.
The decision by the government to allow Petro-Canada to raise equity directly from individual investors is not a product of ideology. It involves a lot of common sense.
Ideology, though, is at the root of much of the opposition that we are hearing. Many members opposite will oppose this legislation based on the belief that state ownership is an end in itself, that it is better to have a weak state owned company than a strong company owned by individual Canadians. Surely it is this glorification of state ownership for its own sake, regardless of its consequences, which is inconsistent with Canadian traditions.
This legislation is good for Petro-Canada. It is good for hard-pressed Canadian taxpayers and those Canadians who, like myself, are concerned about the debt burden we are leaving for the next generation. It is good for Canada since it will allow Petro-Canada to get on with the job of securing our energy future. That is why I support its passage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words on the bill which proposes the privatization of Petro-Canada. We on this side of the House have indicated our opposition to this privatization. We think that at this critical time in the history of our country, with the problems facing the Canadian economy and the uncertainty of oil supplies because of the events in the Middle East, this certainly is not the time to be privatizing Petro-Canada.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin, who indicated that he was opposed to the government using closure or time allocation. I hope that, if the government ever moves it again, and I am sure that after his words, the government will not move to try to close down debate on such a massive, important issue as the privatization of Petro-Canada, he will vote against any move by the House leader on the government side to move in that direction.
This is a very important bill; it is a very important issue. Petroleum products are to the economy of a country what red blood is to the health of a human being. Because of the uncertainty back in 1973 and the first oil shocks of that year and again in 1980, the government of
Government Orders
the day moved to establish a national petroleum corporation.
I had the opportunity of working on the committee which studied the bill to set up this corporation. At the time I do not believe we thought that the corporation would be as large as it is today. We saw it more as an instrument for exploration and development. It has moved on, through successive governments, to expand into the retail trade.
I was surprised, when the present government came to office in 1984, that one of the first things it did was to spend almost $1 billion to buy the downstream assets of Gulf Canada. Surely after all of the uncertainty of the Clark regime in 1979 as to whether it would privatize, partly privatize or not privatize Petro-Canada, it was amazing to me that the government bought up the Gulf Canada gas stations in eastern Canada. At the same time, I believe it provided assistance to the Reichmann organization to buy the upstream resources of Gulf Canada by giving them a tax credit. So, in fact, through that marvellous device known as the Little Egypt bump, the Reichmanns were able to acquire those assets with a great deal of the cost being borne by the taxpayers of Canada.
So given the Tory philosophy and position, it is really amazing that they spent $1 billion dollars, buying up a bunch of gas stations when they could have been committing that $1 billion to exploration and development. Nobody has quite ever explained exactly why they did that.
Now we hear them talking about selling off 15 per cent of the Petro-Canada assets in order to provide $500 million worth of funds that are really needed, according to Wilbert Hopper, President and Chief Executive Officer of Petro-Canada for oil and gas exploration and development. It seems to me that if they are needed now, the Tories might have been better to have saved those dollars back in 1984 and 1985 when they spent almost $1 billion. If it had not spent the money in that way, by giving a tax advantage to the Reichmann organization to purchase the upstream resources of Gulf Canada, it probably would have had all of the operating capital that was required at that time.
Clearly this proposal will not work if the government's plan is to sell off 15 per cent of the shares. No investor I know wants to buy into an organization that is as volatile as the oil industry. All you have to do is look at the

Government Orders
lay-offs announced today by Imperial Oil of from 3,000 to 4,000 employees to know just how volatile that industry is. I do not know that many investors want to invest in a Crown corporation of which 15 per cent will be sold. It makes for a very unhappy wedding, if there is one.
The investors are concerned that the government would use the Crown corporation for its own purpose as an instrument of public policy. It is not very workable to do that because the shareholders are supposed to be protected, but they are still with an 85 per cent interest.
Naturally the privatized corporation is going to be very interested in the views and the position of the minister of industry or the Minister of Finance, whoever holds the shares for the federal government. I do not think that kind of arrangement is ever going to be very happy for investors and probably not very happy for the government. It has been tried in other jurisdictions and usually has been a dismal failure, as it was in the case of B.C. when it tried its B.C. resources privatization scheme.
If ever there was bad timing for the sale of Petro-Can-ada, it surely must be now. The price of oil has gone from $16 or $17 a barrel to over $40 a barrel today. Shares of Petro-Canada, if they were on the market, clearly would be up because their resources in the ground would likewise be up. But the need for security of supply must be weighing heavily on the mind of the minister of energy these days.
Our reserves in the western sedimentary basin have been reduced almost annually. We are committed under the free trade agreement with the United States, regardless of what the oil shocks are-if war broke out in the Middle East today, as it could-to maintain our level of supply to the U.S. With those resources dwindling day after day, how is it possible for a government to sell off PetroCan, which can be a massive instrument of public policy? You only have to look at the percentage of the reserves and a market of something around 20 per cent, which if sold, is gone forever. We have already made a commitment under the FTA that it will be a total market situation. The instruments that the government has left for enunciating or having an energy policy are all being
given away. This is a very important instrument we have now and it will be given away if this bill passes.
The government has said that it wants to privatize this company so that it will gain more capital from the marketplace for exploration and development. I have already asked, why did the government buy a bunch of gas stations if it wanted more money. Why did it spend $1 billion only four years ago to buy a bunch of gas stations if it was really short of capital for exploration and development? But the Canadian capital markets are only so large.
We are having difficulty finding capital resources for the manufacturing industry, the mining industry, for transportation, for all kinds of needs in areas like mine in northern Ontario. Yet it is proposed to privatize this and suck up those scarce financial resources from the Canadian marketplace into Petro-Canada.
Likewise, if Petro-Canada is privatized and these resources go into Petro-Canada, where will these other sectors of the industry, which are not as profitable at some stages, go? Clearly the mining industry is in a terrible state because the government has removed the flow-through shares and the MEDA incentive program.
Only a few weeks ago a number of members of our caucus had meetings in Kirkland Lake and we heard how that whole exploration and development for the mining industry has been destroyed in the last year because of the flow-through shares and the incentive programs are not there. They cannot get resources, if Petro-Canada moves into the marketplace to scrounge up even more resources, that industry and other industries, manufacturing and processing will be even that much more strapped.
The alternative under this bill is that 25 per cent can be sold off to foreign investors. Already we are seeing a dramatic reduction in the Canadian control of the oil industry. If we look at the downstream resources between 1985 and 1989, Canadian control has dropped from 42.7 per cent to 36.1 per cent.
Imagine, Mr. Speaker, in just four years with the Tory government in power, we have seen a 6 per cent-more than that actually, 6.5 per cent-decline in Canadian control of downstream energy resources. It is happening

in many other areas because what the government is saying is that it does not matter who controls. The oil companies with their headquarters in Houston or Chicago or wherever will be just as interested in Canadians as they will be in Americans.
Well, one does not have to be very wise to know that that is simply not the case. When the American administration in Washington, whether it is the Congress or the Senate, or the President, put the twist on the arm of corporate America, it responds. There is no question about it. If we look at the review of upstream resources between 1986 and 1989, a period of only three years, Canadian control has slipped from 49 per cent to 39 per cent, a drop of 10 per cent. If this bill goes through and there are not Canadian funds available to invest in those shares, naturally they will look to the United States for those resources.
One of the reasons that we wanted to establish Petro-Canada back in the seventies was to provide a window on the industry. We know it is controlled by five, six, or seven big oil companies operating internationally. We know that most of those, with the exception of Shell, are headquartered in the United States. We wanted to have, not only to have an instrument of public policy, but a window on that industry to have some influence on it and to know if there is a rip-off taking place.
People in my constituency complain about the high price of oil. Petro-Canada is a window and has been a window on the industry, not only at home, but abroad. Mr. Hopper is the President of the Canadian Petroleum Association. How much closer can you get to the industry than to have that position in Calgary?
Under this proposal, I predict that the national petroleum corporation, Petro-Canada, will cease to be a window on an industry where we know that in 10 or 20 years the level of resources are simply not going to be there. We have seen the level of reserves in the western sedimentary basin dropping all the time. That window could be lost.
In connection with that, in international affairs, we lose. We have Petro-Canada International which has been a valuable instrument for assisting Third World countries to develop their petroleum resources. Surely we, as a nation, have a responsibility through CIDA, international development agencies, the NGOs, and so on, to assist in international development. Petro-Canada
Government Orders
has been a valuable instrument in that regard. Surely, Third World development is helping them to develop their resources. We did it, along with other countries, in India and other countries to develop their green revolution back in the sixties to see them able to grow their new varieties of dwarf wheat so that they could become self-sufficient or at least able to feed themselves.
Surely, petroleum is the life-blood of any economy. Assisting Third World countries to develop their mineral and energy resources is a valuable aspect. That will be lost under this proposal, the ability of Petro-Canada to be a window on the petroleum industry, not only in the nation, but abroad, and also to be an important international instrument for the development of Third World energy.
Petro-Canada has been the instrument of public policy development for projects such as Hibernia. I believe that the exact percentage of the development of Hibernia is 25 per cent owned by Petro-Canada. Surely, to throw that over into the private sector will not ensure the development of Hibernia. What about the others: Terra Nova, 44 per cent owned by Petro-Canada; OSLO, 15 per cent owned by Petro-Canada; Syncrude, 17 per cent owned by Petro-Canada; and the Wolf Lake project, 50 per cent owned by Petro-Canada. Those are projects that governments have difficulty in knowing exactly how to approach those and what percentage to be involved.
How can we be sure that, if Petro-Canada is privatized, these important projects which the government is committed to will go ahead? How will its share in OSLO or whatever simply be sold off? Ultimately, if privatization takes place, investors will not be satisfied with 15 per cent. Investors simply will want 100 per cent private sector to be sure that it is not an instrument of public policy. The ability of government to invest soundly and wisely in these projects will be lost and the responsibility for doing it will be lost.
The government has got a lot to answer for in proposing this at a time when oil prices on the world scene have risen from $16 or $18 a barrel during the past year to over $42 a barrel now. Can we be sure that the government knows what it is doing by privatizing this? Can we be sure that consumers are not going to be ripped off at the gas pump?

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the city of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island should be designated as the "Birthplace of Canada" to mark the one hundred and twenty-fifth anniversary of the 1864 Charlottetown Conference of the Fathers of Confederation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of satisfaction and pride to move and begin debate on this motion.
I am very happy to have had my motion chosen in the draw at this time. I feel that most Canadians do not understand the order in which motions and Private Members' bills appear for debate because it is chosen by
Private Members' Business
lottery, better known as the luck of the draw. Of course, I am going to need much more than luck to see this motion through to completion.
As the member of Parliament for Hillsborough, I have worked since June 1989 to achieve this designation and, of course, there have been many, many Islanders who have worked much longer than this to see Charlottetown given the recognition it deserves.
In 1989 the 125th anniversary of the Charlottetown Conference was celebrated. In 1864 at the conference, delegates from Canada and the Maritimes agreed in principle to form one union, the Dominion of Canada. At this time in Charlottetown a feeling of excitement and endless possibility was born. Delegates representing several provinces decided to form one nation. They realized that in unity, there is strength. Today, in 1990, Canadians hope to recapture that sense of unity and optimism.
It is possible to recapture the atmosphere of the 1864 conference if you walk around Charlottetown. Charlottetown is a community which was already 100 years old when the conference took place. You can begin this by walking up Great George Street from the harbour, the route followed by the Fathers of Confederation, the route they took after they disembarked from their steamer, Queen Victoria. Trees shade the area, and as you walk through the trees, Province House comes into view. Province House is where the conference took place, and it is where today the legislative proceedings of the province take place.
Province House is a great source of pride to Prince Edward Islanders. It was built as the colonial house between 1843 and 1846, with the official opening in January 1847. It has served as the seat of government from that time onward. It is a beautiful but aging building, and the aging of the building led to an agreement between the federal and provincial governments in 1974 to restore many of the rooms in Province House to the 1800s. This job was completed in 1986.
The room that most people want to see as they visit this building is the red chamber, the chamber in which the Fathers of Confederation met.
The National Capital Commission has worked with the province of Prince Edward Island in recognition of the role that the provincial capitals play in the evolution of the country. The commission has created direct linkages with Charlottetown in recognition of its valued role as

October 11, 1990
Private Members' Business
the historic and symbolic capital in the creation of Confederation.
Through a cultural exchange program, Charlottetown and Prince Edward Island were made more visible in Canada's capital; and the national capital is now more familiar to the residents of Prince Edward Island. Their efforts help to highlight the potential educational importance of debating this motion.
Canadians need unifying symbols. We need to be reminded of our great past so that we can think of the future with hope. I am afraid that if we do not make an active effort to affirm our identity as Canadians, to affirm the reasons why this country was created in the first place, we could lose it by default. That would be a tragedy, with such greatness behind us and so much to look forward to.
Canadians desire to renew the bonds that hold us together, to regain a sense of nationhood, as is evidenced by the huge numbers of people who come here to Parliament Hill. They come here not only to watch their democracy in action, but to see a building which symbolizes the nation. The Parliament Buildings and this Chamber, in particular, command our respect and our pride. And I do not think anyone leaves this Hill untouched.
Dignified and treasured as these buildings are, they are only part of the story of Canada. I think that Canadians should experience the same sense of history in Charlottetown as they do here in Ottawa. While any Islander knows the story of the Dominion's birth, and is happy to tell it to visitors, we would appreciate the support and the resources of the Government of Canada in letting all Canadians know about it and experience it.
Canadians learn in school that Charlottetown was the location of the conference where Confederation was born. What they might not realize is that Charlottetown's streets and buildings bring these history lessons to life. Many homes and buildings that date from that era still exist and have been fully restored to give Canadians a true sense of the times. One mansion, at which some of the delegates stayed while in Charlottetown, has been declared a national landmark. Government House, the home of Prince Edward Island's Lieutenant Governor,
has been preserved beautifully. And the home of William Pope, one of Prince Edward Island's Fathers of Confederation, is now designated as a national park. Also, some modem landmarks commemorate this important moment in Canadian history and add to Charlottetown's appeal, such as the Confederation Centre of the Arts, the living monument to Canada's founding fathers.
All of this was accomplished through the dedication of many Islanders and many other people over a period of many years, such as the Charlottetown Area Development Corporation, through the Charlottetown Area Beautification Project, city council, members of the Legislative Assembly and the Heritage Foundation of Canada, as well as the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada. The people of Charlottetown are conscious of their historic surroundings and they have worked very hard to maintain the physical aspects, and as a result, the spirit of the Charlottetown conference.
Mr. Speaker, I could stand here all day and list the individuals whose contributions to this effort have made it worth while. But, one person who stands out in my mind is a person by the name of Eddy Rice. Over the past year, I have sought the input and the advice of many people regarding this type of motion and their help was invaluable to me. But Eddie Rice, who has worked to preserve and promote Charlottetown's special place in history, was one of the first people to discuss this idea with me, so I especially appreciate his role. I think he summed it up best when he said: "We are guardians of our own heritage".
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that, due to a drafting oversight, my motion now reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the city of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island should be designated as the "Birthplace of Canada" to mark the one hundred and twenty-fifth anniversary of the 1864 Charlottetown Conference of the Fathers of Confederation.
Later in the debate, my hon. colleague, the hon. member for Cardigan, will rise and move an amendment to this motion. The amendment will change the words "Birthplace of Canada" to "Birthplace of Confederation".
October 11, 1990

Mr. Speaker, on September 27 of this year, during Routine Proceedings, I moved for leave to introduce Bill C-330, An Act to Commemorate the Birthplace of Confederation. This was agreed to, the bill was read the first time and ordered to be printed.
This bill would promote the unifying symbols in the history of Canada in a time when the country seems divided. The bill shall, by means of plaques or other signs or in any other suitable manner mark the sites and buildings where was held, prior to 1867, the Charlottetown Conference, during which delegates from the Maritimes and from Canada agreed to explore the possibility of one union.
It is my hope that all members of this House will support both my motion and my bill. Prince Edward Islanders have worked for the official designation of their capital city, not only out of a desire to preserve and enhance its unique historic role but also to strengthen the local and the provincial economy which, I am sure, all hon. members know is in great need of strengthening. Prince Edward Island's economy is based, to a great extent, on tourism.
According to the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, in 1989 over 740,000 people visited P.E.I. That is a large number of people for a province with a population of about 130,000. P.E.I.'s tourism sector must continue to grow so that its economy will be strengthened. Tourism is a very competitive sector, and we know we can compete. To do so, we need the help of the Government of Canada.
The official designation of Charlottetown would be of great help in this competitive market appealing not only to Canadian visitors, but to international ones as well. With increased tourism comes increased activity in all areas of the economy. P.E.I.'s existing tourism base presents Canada with a wonderful opportunity to showcase a very special event in our history.
Canada was created in a way which would be known around the world as the Canadian way of doing things. Delegates gathered in an atmosphere of hospitality and optimism. Meetings were held and vital business was conducted. Also, festivities took place. Festive dinners and parties were enjoyed by all. This has become a famous image of the conference. In September 1864, Charlottetown was the place to be, and the following
Private Members' Business
quote from a letter by Charlottetown conference delegate, George Brown, to his wife, Anne, will help to give a visual view of the hospitality and optimism.
"Amid most beautiful scenery, we came suddenly on the capital city of the island. Our steamer dropped anchor magnificently in the stream, and its man-of-war cut evidently inspired the natives with huge respect for their big brothers from Canada. I flatter myself we did that well. Having dressed ourselves in the correct style- we pulled away for shore and landed like Mr. Christopher Columbus."
In fact, the S.S. Queen Victoria had caused some alarm that morning when it entered Hillsborough Bay because it had been mistaken for a Yankee commerce raider. With this auspicious beginning, the Charlottetown Conference was under way, and the discussions of the delegates at that conference shaped the lives of Canadians for the past 126 years. That is why I stand here today asking for the support of this House.
The conference was originally planned as a discussion of a possible federation of the maritime provinces, but when the Canadian delegation arrived, it turned into a discussion of a much larger scheme, the federation of British North America. The delegates heard speeches by John A. Macdonald, George Cartier, Thomas D'Arcy McGee, George Brown and many others. The debate was lively. Before the delegates left the Island in 1864, the government and the citizens of Charlottetown threw a gala ball at Province House where they danced, dined and made fine speeches until the wee hours of the morning. The ball was recreated in 1989 on the 125th anniversary during a memorable party in the streets surrounding Province House.
If there was ever a time when Canadians needed living symbols of their history and an understanding that nation building is not over, it is now. I urge the people in this Chamber to support this motion. It would be a simple gesture, but an important one for Prince Edward Islanders and for all Canadians.
I would like to conclude with a quote from one of Prince Edward Island's delegates to the convention, and Father of Confederation, Thomas Heath Haviland. He said: "Never was there such an important meeting as this held before in the history of British America; and it may yet be said that here, in little Prince Edward Island, was

October 11, 1990
Private Members' Business
that union formed which has produced one of the greatest nations on the face of God's earth."
I urge all members to support this motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to speak to this motion of the hon. member for Hillsborough.
Most of us recognize the importance of the Charlottetown Conference. In our grade school history class we learned about the great deeds done by people like John Hamilton Gray, George Coles, and others. When Canadians like Sir John A. Macdonald and George Etienne Cartier landed at Peakes Wharf in Charlottetown, little did they know how important their actions were. Indeed many people could learn today from the example of Canada's founding fathers.
The Charlottetown Conference was originally intended to be a discussion on the form of Maritime Union but then the Canadians arrived and they never looked back. Dr. Francis Bolger, an authority on the Charlottetown Conference, said:
The Charlottetown Conference was indeed a success. The 23 delegates reached an agreement on the desirability of Confederation and on the general outline of a future constitution. Perhaps more importantly, they dedicated themselves to the establishment of a new nation. Subsequent conferences in Quebec City and London, England, formalized, refined and systematized the constitutional principles agreed upon in Charlottetown, and in 1867 the Dominion of Canada was formed.
Despite the great importance that we place on the Charlottetown Conference there is no official recognition of Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation. What the motion does is encourage the House to designate, in law, that Charlottetown is indeed the birthplace of Confederation.
The city of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, is a beautiful city with a remarkable sense of history. There are plaques in front of Province House, the sight of the conference, commemorating those Islanders that participated in the Charlottetown Conference of 1864. The plaques list the many achievements of the men who helped found this great nation. The time has come for the federal government to recognize formally that Charlottetown is the birthplace of Confederation.
The federal government could play a special role in helping develop historical sights in and around the city related to the events of 1864. Using the resources of Environment Canada and the Department of Communications, much can be done in and around Charlottetown to help preserve, restore, and revive many of the places associated with the conference. Sights like Government House and Pope House have been restored to their original condition, allowing for a vivid recollection of the history. Much has been done recently around Peakes Wharf where the delegates to the conference landed, restoring old shops and the like. Such restorations have added much to the life of Charlottetown and attract many visitors.
Recognition of the historical role in Canadian history played by Charlottetown would help strengthen the local economy. Prince Edward Island relies more heavily on tourism as a supplier of money and employment than any other province. With careful promotion of Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation many more Canadians who have yet to enjoy the history and spirit of Prince Edward Island will come to visit the Island.
It must be remembered that a move to commemorate the Charlottetown Conference will not only affect the city itself, but it will have a lasting impact on the tourism industry on the whole Island.
As the 125th anniversary of Confederation approaches in 1992 Canadians should become more aware of the history surrounding the great event. It has been said that Canada was a "noble experiment", and nothing could be more true today. As we look around and see the tensions that have built up, we find a Canada in need of unifying symbols. Recognition of Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation would be such a symbol, and I encourage all members to support the motion of the hon. member for Hillsborough.
Before I end my remarks I would like to move an amendment to the motion to correct a minor error.
Therefore I move:
That, in the opinion of this House, the city of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island should be designated as the "Birthplace of Confederation" to mark the one hundred and twenty-fifth anniversary of the 1864 Charlottetown Conference of the Fathers of Confederation.
