speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me congratulate you on your position in the chair here today. This is the first time I have had an opportunity to speak in the House when you have been in the chair, so I congratulate you on your appointment.
I am honoured to participate in this debate in the House of Commons today and to support the sentiments of my colleague from Hillsborough and thank him for putting forth his motion.
The motion before us today asks that we recognize the importance of a meeting that occurred in Charlottetown almost 126 years ago. The Charlottetown Conference in 1864 was indeed a pivotal event in the history of Canada. It saw the leaders of the emerging Dominion of Canada come together to propose the founding of a new country. That initial meeting led to Confederation and eventually to Canada as we know it-Canada from sea to sea and from the 49th parallel to the far-flung reaches of the Arctic.
Those leaders, the Fathers of Confederation, had a vision. It was a revolutionary vision, one of disparate colonies uniting to form a strong young nation with a great future. Above all, it was a vision of a new way of doing things.
Here were the representatives of two peoples from two homelands, England and France. They saw the opportunity to reach out to one another, to unite for mutual benefit, and to live together in peace and mutual respect. At Charlottetown, in 1864, the idea of a country
Private Members' Business
of people who would stand together while embracing their differences was bom.
Over the decades Canadians have enlarged and enriched this vision. In our way we are giving new meaning to that concept of partnership of all regions and citizens of this country.
There is no doubt that the Charlottetown Conference was a key step in our evolution as a nation. I want to agree with the hon. member for Hillsborough and also the hon. member for Cardigan who has moved am appropriate and accurate amendment to the motion to call Charlottetown the birthplace of Confederation rather than the birthplace of Canada. With the amendment to the motion I want to say that I endorse this motion whole-heartedly.
I was doing some research on who were some of the renowned persons bom in Charlottetown. One of the Fathers of Confederation, George Coles, was bom in Charlottetown. The son of one of the Fathers of Confederation, Sir Joseph Pope, was born in Charlottetown. The present Lieutenant-Governor, Marion Reid, was bom in Charlottetown. Our friend, journalist Mike Duffy, has Charlottetown as his birthplace. The former environment minister in the previous Parliament, the hon. Tom McMillan, was bom in Charlottetown. It is as well as the birthplace of the great story Anne of Green Gables.
Confederation is the heart and the soul of Canada. It was by no means an easy road that our forefathers had to take. It was the road of compromise, of accommodation, of seeking the middle ground. Those were the principles upon which this country was built. Those are the principles which still guide us and which we must still honour.
This is the fair, the decent, the Canadian way. This is the legacy that was born in Charlottetown in 1864.
When our forebears came together for the Charlottetown Conference and at a subsequent conference in Quebec City, they had to grapple with some very difficult issues. In those days there were only a few provinces that were involved in those discussions. There were delegates from the three maritime provinces, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and there were representatives from Upper and Lower Canada which encompassed what is now Ontario and Quebec.
It was a much smaller geographical entity than Canada is today. Nevertheless, the Fathers of Confederation

October 11, 1990
Private Members' Business
under the leadership of Sir John A. Macdonald faced the task of bringing together small sparsely populated communities scattered over immense distances. These communities also were divided by different economic interests and by different cultural, linguistic, legal and educational traditions.
How could they form a union while still satisfying local and regional interests? How could they accommodate the aspirations of both French and English speaking peoples in one political entity?
To remain separate colonies was to risk being swallowed up by our neighbour in the south. To merge completely and to try to submerge our differences would have meant losing the diversity already of great significance in those early days.
There was only one acceptable answer: a federation, a union that gave us a strong central government and Parliament and an ample measure of self-government and autonomy for each of the federating provinces.
How did our ancestors work out the details of that alliance? It was by sitting down together, debating, negotiating, and compromising.
Let us remember that the British North America Act, our Confederation document, guaranteed certain language and education rights and Quebec's system of civil law. Subsequent generations would have to improve on these arrangements.
Confederation was not a one-time event. Indeed it is an ongoing, evolutionary process. The partnerships that Canadians formed with one another in the early days of our history had to be renegotiated, renewed, and refined over the years.
Canadian historian, Senator Eugene Forsey, put it this way in an article that he wrote in 1962:
The Fathers wrought well, and laid our foundations deep and strong. But the building is still unfinished and parts of it have suffered some damage through the years. It does not need a bombing squad or a wrecking crew. But it does need alterations, repairs, additions, the expansion of certain rooms; and all of us must be made to feel at home in it.
Since 1867 we have seen many constitutional milestones. Each round of constitutional talks had its heartwrench-ing moments as Canadians confronted their differences and sought common ground in the complex maze of competing interests and priorities.
Yet the unifying vision prevailed. We Canadians maintained our faith in the process that our ancestors set in motion.
From those first dreams of our ancestors of a daring new national experiment, Canada has grown to become an ever more mature, fair, and caring society. Nations around the world admire us for our principles and traditions.
We are known as peace-loving, tolerant, generous. We were not bom with these characteristics-we honed them through the process of learning to live together, of standing up for one another through the long haul.
In 1864, in Charlottetown, our ancestors conceived of the idea of Canada-one nation created out of a collection of colonies.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is vital to celebrate the Charlottetown Conference of 1864, to acknowledge the role it played in the birth of Confederation. Looking back on those times helps us gain a better understanding of the constitutional processes that will continue for many years to come.
It is up to all Canadians to continue the work of reaching out to one another, of building a new climate of understanding that can be fulfilled by the faith and goodwill of every citizen of this country.
As we stand on the threshold of the 21st century, we continue to strive for a strong and prosperous Canada for all citizens, mindful of the first discussions and decisions made in Charlottetown, at the birthplace of our Confederation.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join this debate and congratulate the member of Parliament for Hillsborough who has tabled this bill for our discussion today.
I guess I should state at the outset my vested interest in seeing that this particular matter is proceeded with. It goes back many years to my grandfather, who was bom in Charlottetown, and of course my dad, who was bom in that great province as well. So I state at the outset my vested interest, but I do want to compliment the member of Parliament for Hillsborough as well as his colleague for Cardigan who has put forward an amendment which I am supporting, and I know other members on this side of
October 11, 1990

the House, as well as on the government side, have now indicated their support.
I would like to pay tribute particularly to the parliamentary secretaiy who has just spoken. I found her words both eloquent and timely, and very fitting. I am happy to see that a government representative has taken the time to participate in this very worth-while debate, in assuring that this particular measure can proceed and proceed with despatch.
The Charlottetown Conference, like many events in history, was the result of precedents and accidents, the outcome of which few could have foreseen. While the conference was held ostensibly to debate the possibilities of a maritime union, a greater purpose soon unfolded.
Two-thirds of the Canadian cabinet had boarded the Canadian government steamer Queen Victoria in late August and sailed from Quebec to Charlottetown. They carried with them far-reaching proposals for Confederation.
I would like to quote a passage which an author wrote with regard to the voyage to Charlottetown:
From Gaspe our course was direct to Charlottetown, the little capital of little Prince Edward Island. I was up at four in the morning! -Thursday morning (September 1)-to see the sun rise and have a salt water bath. We had just reached the westerly point of Prince Edward and were running along the coast of as pretty a country as you ever put your eye upon-About noon we came to an inlet which we entered, and running up for some miles what appeared to be a river but was in fact but an inlet of the sea (Hillsborough Bay), amid most beautiful scenery, we came suddenly on the Capital City of the Island.
That describes clearly the voyage which took place from the Gaspe to Charlottetown. Twenty-three statesmen and three secretaries sat down at a massive mahogany table in the legislative council chamber in the graceful Georgian Province House.
John A. Macdonald and Cartier began by setting out the general arguments in favour of Confederation with a broad outline of the Canadian proposal. They sought to show that such a union of the provinces was indeed possible. Confederation promised something that Maritime union could not, a trans-continental country. Their purpose, shaped by a faith and the power of hope over adversity.
Private Members' Business
The Charlottetown Conference thus laid the foundation upon which Confederation was built. It was in Charlottetown that the grand plans of the statesmen who were to become known as the Fathers of Confederation were first given practical shape. Perhaps the most remarkable achievement of the whole conference was the conversion of a significant proportion of the Maritime delegates to the cause of Confederation. For the sake of Confederation not a few would put at stake their political careers and in some cases even their personal reputations.
The Charlottetown Conference gave the delegates a sense of common destiny and a devotion to a cause greater than their local loyalties.
It is, therefore, Mr. Speaker, fitting that this city, this great little city, which saw the high hopes and quiet labours of our political forbears develop into a great community of peoples be recognized as the "Birthplace of Confederation".
The challenges the Fathers of Confederation faced over a century ago are challenges that we in this Chamber and across this great land continue to confront. Nonetheless, we can draw from their example and from their example. The imagination, the determination, and, yes, the courage that distinguished their great effort 125 years ago is needed anew.
Surely the hope of our country lies, just as it did in Charlottetown in 1864, in the acceptance of our differences and, Mr. Speaker, as you will well know, our distinctiveness; and in the recognition of our common problems and our common purpose.
That is what Macdonald, Cartier, John Gray of Prince Edward Island, Tilley from New Brunswick, and, yes, a fellow Nova Scotian by the name of Tupper and other distinguished statesmen had in mind in Charlottetown in 1864, when beneath the old gas lamps in the Provincial Building they committed themselves to a new political arrangement of the British North American colonies.
Today the country these men dreamed of has matured into one of the great and to some extent untapped bountiful countries of the world. It is a country of talent and opportunity, a country civilized in its human relations, a country rich in culture and literature.
Canada is not just a few acres of snow, but a country of immensely varied beauty of landscape and season, of
October 11, 1990

Private Members' Business
people from a hundred worldly professions who now call Canada their home, of valued diversity and of rights and privileges envied throughout the world.
Apart from honouring Charlottetown as the "Cradle of Confederation", we ought, perhaps as a Chamber and as humble representatives, honour the efforts of our 19th century nation builders by demonstrating, as so ably put by the parliamentary secretary, that we have a vision of how Canada can grow and evolve in response to the different and difficult times ahead.
Considerations of the new agenda remain unfinished. It is up to all of us to propose solutions and to chart the new course. To be involved in that effort is to be involved with the same spirit that fired the imagination and efforts of the Fathers of Confederation at Charlottetown almost 125 years ago.
With great humility, it is my pleasure to participate in this debate and join with my colleagues, the four members of Parliament from Charlottetown, in supporting them and the government in their quest to have Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation of this great nation.

Mr. Speaker, I too am very pleased to be able to speak today on this motion put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Hillsborough, and amended by my colleague the hon. member for Cardigan, on designating Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation.
First I want to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Hillsborough in taking the initiative in introducing this motion before the House. I feel that it is very appropriate that we are discussing the designation of Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation here on the floor of the House of Commons, for it is here that we plan for the future of our country. It is only fitting that it is here that we recognize where our country was planned.
In identifying Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation, it is both a recognition and an acceptance of the importance of our historical heritage. We have listened to colleagues this afternoon speak of the events of the Charlottetown Conference of 1864 and how those events have helped shape the future of the country. I congratulate each one of them for their comments.
There are numerous reasons why the official designation of Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation would be beneficial. Today in the time allotted to me I would like to deal with three of these reasons.
First, and most important, Canada needs to officially identify historical events. This identification will help all of us develop our national pride.
Second, at a time when our country has become somewhat divided, it is imperative that we concentrate and celebrate those events which bind us together as a nation.
Third, not only will this designation of Charlottetown contribute to the well-being of our country, but there is no doubt it will contribute to the well-being of my province of Prince Edward Island.
I believe that we can continue to learn a great deal from those early Fathers of Confederation who met for ten days in Charlottetown 126 years ago and found compromise among their differences.
It was the Charlottetown Conference that really set Confederation in motion. Maritime union had long been talked about in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island. In fact, in March of 1864, all three legislatures passed resolutions to have a conference to discuss it. Nothing happened until after the June, 1864 and the constitutional crisis of the province of Canada, when the Canadians asked to attend the conference to propose a union of all British North America.
The request at first rather staggered the Maritime governments, but then the place and date of the meeting were selected: Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, September 1 to 9, 1864. It might be of interest to members of the House to know that at the time of the conference, Charlottetown was the eleventh largest city in British North America.
At the conference, Maritime union was virtually dropped and the delegates agreed on the outline of a scheme for a more general union. It was the Charlottetown Conference which produced the momentum which was so obvious at the Quebec conference in October and so necessary to carry Confederation.
Prince Edward Islanders have learned a great deal from their heritage and affiliation with the Fathers of Confederation. All Canadians should be able to commemorate the birthplace of Confederation and under-
October 11, 1990

stand the events, the players, and the location of the activities to comprehend fully our national heritage.
As Canadians, we have long sought after some prepackaged identity, often disregarding the facts of our own history which contribute to our true make-up and, therefore, our identity. This past year of our nation's history has been one of conflict within our confederation. It is now more important than ever that we look to our past for strength and, in some cases, direction for the future.
We need to feel patriotic about our great country and Charlottetown has a moral obligation to help. It has the stage.
At times, we often look toward the United States, not for guidance but because of the simple fact that it seems to be able to produce patriotism on command. It has been pointed out that at different times within the year, Washington is packed with school children from all over the United States. They also travel to Philadelphia and come from everywhere in the United States. Canadian school children could travel to Charlottetown, to learn and to see where, what, and how Canada was conceived. In doing so, they would have a better grasp of our country's beginnings and a better grasp of their national heritage and identity.
As an Islander, I am proud of the beauty and historical importance of our provincial capital, Charlottetown. It is truly an exceptional city. The older part of the city includes our provincial legislature, known as Province House, where the meetings were held in 1864. It also includes stately mansions, refurbished shops, and commercial buildings dating from the last century which line the streets. It is possible to walk and see exactly where the Fathers of Confederation spent their time.
Charlottetown has received national recognition before. In 1964, people in Canada showed enough faith in their history that they built the Confederation Centre for the Arts in Charlottetown as a memorial to the founding of Canada. This concrete and glass complex comprises a theatre, a splendid gallery, and the provincial archives. Each year, as part of the much acclaimed Charlottetown Festival, the flexible 1,000 seat theatre holds a revival of
Private Members' Business
the musical based on the island novel, Anne of Green Gables.
There is no question that the designation of Charlottetown will help improve our provincial economy. It is distinctive among Canadian cities as being the birthplace of Confederation and that represents an important tourism resource whose development has the potential for bringing benefits to the entire province.
I realize that you are telling me, Mr. Speaker, that my time is up. I just want to close by once again commending the hon. member for Hillsborough in his initiative on this issue. I am proud and honoured to have the opportunity to address and support the designation of Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today in debate on my colleague's motion. I am an islander as well, but I am not from Prince Edward Island. I am from another island called Cape Breton Island. Those islands in the east have had great historical significance in the development of the northern part of North America.
As anybody who has visited Prince Edward Island knows-and it is not that far from Cape Breton Island- the people there are among the finest in this great nation. That little town of Charlottetown is something unique. There is a special ambience that is there. I am not quite sure how one would properly describe it.
When one looks at the island itself, the island of Prince Edward Island, it truly is like a rolling pillow of lush green in the summertime, with the surf that pounds in on its miles of sandy coastline being like a braid that defines it. The capital city of Charlottetown is like an emerald on the coastline.
It is little wonder that when men and women of vision over 125 years ago pulled into that harbour that something took over their spirit. My colleague from Cape Breton-East Richmond read a passage which I think was very appropriate. They stopped talking about what could not be done and started to dream the impossible. At that time, the impossible was a nation called Canada.
For some reason, Charlottetown has perhaps hallowed soil. Maybe it has always had a destiny. I do not know. Some people believe in that. For some strange reason, the political divisions and the difficulty of geography we still face today-think of it. This was 126 years ago.

October 11, 1990
Private Members' Business
Today, we talk about how vast the country is. Today, we talk about the problems between our regions. Today, we talk about the problems between our languages. This was 126 years ago. There were no airplanes, no telephones, and no cars. There were boats, horses, and wagons. There were great distances. For some reason, Charlottetown pulled all those positive energies together and let those men and women dream the impossible, put aside their differences, and forge the great nation that is Canada.
I have had many opportunities to go to Charlottetown and Prince Edward Island and I go back as often as I can. These are times of great trouble in our land with the great divisions politically, economically, and linguistically across the country. Once we get this motion through and the designation comes for Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation, maybe for every future constitutional conference, when everybody does their agenda, they want to do their horse-trading, and they want to make sure that their needs are at the top of the agenda, maybe we should make it compulsory that our leaders from across Canada take a little trip to Charlottetown. They should walk the streets, go into the buildings where those meetings took place, and think about the history that was created. Men and women 126 years ago put their differences aside and stopped talking about what could not be done and started to talk about what could be done.
Maybe, just maybe, they should do the same thing and go to L'Anse-au-Meadow in Newfoundland where the first people landed. Then maybe they should go to the Citadel in Quebec so that when they all get together that infectious spirit, that special something, that little bit of magic that Charlottetown has caused for all Canadians, will be a little infectious.
I am very proud that my colleague, the member for Hillsborough, has had the foresight to put this motion together, and I am so pleased to see the support on both sides of the House. Maybe once again Charlottetown is weaving its magic, because I cannot recall the day, at least recently, when we have had members from all sides of the House getting up and speaking from the heart, and speaking eloquently and positively about a motion that is on the floor and before the Chair of the House of Commons.
I cannot think of any time since I was elected when we have had an hour in which people sat down and put their differences aside, and with the very eloquent remarks of the hon. parliamentary secretary. It gives me reason to feel kind of good.
Maybe, Mr. Speaker, just maybe, that special ambience, that special something that the hon. member for Hillsborough is trying to recognize in this motion, has once again touched this place.
The history of Canada is a history we should all be proud of. But it is a history that many times we forget. It is a history perhaps that we learn in grade school, but it is not one that we carry with us.
There has been mention of the importance of having symbols of national unity and that is important. It is important to remember the positive reasons why we are a nation and why we are together. I cannot think of a more fitting symbol, more pleasant symbol, or a more appropriate symbol of national unity than the city of Charlottetown, that city nestled on the harbour on the east coast of Canada that drew all that energy and drew all those people together.
It would do well for each and every one of us in the House tonight, after we vote in a positive way to proceed with this motion as quickly as we can, to make a commitment that maybe, just maybe, the next time we get a break-and goodness knows, that might be sooner than later-that maybe what we should do is go down to that beautiful city of Charlottetown, the birthplace of Confederation, and have a little walk around. Then maybe the next time we come back and meet in the House, we will get on, not to dismantling and damaging this nation as we are all a little guilty of in some of our partisan comments, but to furthering the cause and building this great nation, Canada.
It gives me a great deal of pleasure to support the motion that is before the Chair today.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity at this time of adjournment to discuss a question which I put in the House on February 23 last in which I asked the Secretary of State about the cuts that took place to native programs in the Secretary of State department. The House will remember that in the budget this year, the Secretary of State made substantial cuts to native representative organizations. In fact, they were cut in many cases by 100 per cent. Cuts were made to native communications programs and, in many cases as well, those native communications programs and native newspapers received cuts of up to 100 per cent, and the same thing happened in native broadcasting.
As usual, the minister gave an unsatisfactory answer to my question. He simply indicated that everybody had to take cuts during a time of budget cutting in order to curb the deficit. But, in this case, he made substantial cuts for a group of people in this country who have not been fairly treated by the Government of Canada and by the people of Canada, and yet seem to be bearing or are being forced by this government to bear the deepest cuts in their programs and, as a result, substantial damage and difficulty was created for the native people of this country. For example, as Mr. Speaker will know, native newspapers have been forced to shut down. One of the most recent shutdowns was at the Micmac News, a newspaper in Atlantic Canada that communicates both between Micmac people and Canadians as a whole. You will know, Mr. Speaker, that that newspaper was the one that was responsible for pressing the case of Donald Marshall, Jr., who was unjustly imprisoned in Nova Scotia for 10 or 11 years for a crime which he did not commit. It was the Micmac News that pressed that case and made the Micmac people and the people of Canada aware of that case and, as a result, a royal commission was struck in Nova Scotia. It found that the justice
Adjournment Debate
system in Nova Scotia was in error, an appeal took place and Donald Marshall was, of course, released from jail.
I think what is even worse is that the cuts to the native programs in the Secretary of State department created some serious difficulties in the relationship between native people in Canada and the Government of Canada and non-natives in Canada. Poor relations during this last summer broke into virtual open civil disobedience and conflict with the people of Canada at Kanesatake and at Kahnawake in the province of Quebec. I think, as a result of those conflicts, the federal government ended up spending tens of millions of dollars, some people have suggested over $100 million, to deal with that conflict through the armed forces and the police forces of Canada and Quebec.
It does not make sense for this government to be constantly attacking native programs and to be constantly cutting native programs even though native people are not the people who are responsible for the huge deficit that this government has sustained. As a result of cutting a few million dollars out of the Secretary of State programs for native people, we ended up destroying good relations between the native people of Canada and the Government of Canada and the non-native people of Canada. As a result, we spent tens of millions of dollars and perhaps over $100 million to send the military into places like Kahnawake and Kanesatake. It simply does not make sense.
It is not good sense from the point of view of economics; it is not good sense from the point of view of cutting the deficit; and it is certainly not good sense from the point of view of maintaining good relations between the native people of Canada, the Government of Canada and non-natives in this country. It is extremely unfortunate that the Secretary of State does not realize that and that the Secretary of State earlier than this did not take steps to restore those programs, native broadcasting, native newspapers and funding for the aboriginal representative organizations that assist in communications between native people and non-native people in this country so that we can have a productive relationship.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening with regard to a matter that I have been raising consistently on the floor of the House of Commons since 1985.
More recently, I had put a question to the Minister of Labour concerning the Program for Older Workers Adjustment. It just so happens that there are a good
number of these individuals in my constituency of Cape Breton-East Richmond who have been attempting since 1985 to become part and parcel of the Program for Older Workers Adjustment.
In 1985, the Minister of Finance announced approximately $200 million to be set aside for a program for older workers adjustment. Thereafter, negotiations were entered into by the provincial and federal governments respectfully, and they came to an understanding whereby individuals would get certain benefits under that program.
Individuals in my constituency, particularly construction workers, have not been able to come within the meaning of these agreements. As a result, as good Canadians that they are, they are being denied the benefits of that particular program. I find it unacceptable that the Government of Canada would deny these individuals the benefits of a program which are supposed to go to older workers. The reality is that on the island of Cape Breton, unemployment is at an all time high. The prospects for employment in the construction industry are as likely as an individual going to go Out and win the million dollar lottery. There are no jobs. The prospects of jobs in the very near future are just not there.
There is a body of individuals who are 50 years of age, 55 and some older who would like to retire with some sense of dignity. Seventy-five per cent of construction workers on Cape Breton Island are unemployed, 75 per cent. There is a need for the Government of Canada to take positive, affirmative action in order to address that particular problem. The Government of Canada blames the province, the province blames the federal government. It happens to be two Tory governments.
Nevertheless, who are the victims? Who are the individuals without these benefits? They are individuals who have paid their taxes to help build our schools, they have built our churches. Now, when they do not have the wherewithal, they seek dignity from the Government of Canada which has said at every turn: "No, no, no".
If they had not put those eight illegal people in the other place, they would have had the money to amend the program for older workers adjustment and to include
October 11, 1990

the construction workers in Cape Breton. They convinced individuals and have convinced the provincial government of their need. The provincial government is now willing to amend the program for older workers adjustment, but the federal government is not prepared to assist in any way.
I want the parliamentary secretary to the minister involved to stand in his place and show some real signs, demonstrable proof that he has compassion, that his government has compassion and understanding for those individuals who have been without the assistance of the program for older workers adjustment.
I raised this issue in 1985, 1986, 1987, 1988, 1989 and 1990 on several different occasions during that time frame. The construction industry itself, the union representatives and others have made repeated representations to the minister involved, as well as some of the other cabinet colleagues who sit around the table.
We are not seeking a billion dollars in new taxes or income for this particular program. We are talking of men and women, perhaps the age of the hon. member opposite, who have children in university and have mortgages to pay. I would ask him, as the parliamentary secretary, for fairness, for compassion, for understanding and for a positive decision to give to those men and to those women in the construction industry a chance to continue their lives with their families and friends and loved ones and to be able to do it with a sense of dignity and pride, knowing that the Government of Canada does care and is prepared to do something about it.
I ask, Mr. Speaker through you, to the parliamentary secretary if he would respond in a positive way.

Mr. Speaker, on June 4 of this year, I asked a question of the Minister of Agriculture regarding the difficult situation faced by dairy farmers not only in British Columbia but virtually right across Canada.
The difficulty concerns the growing loss of revenue, particularly in those communities that are close to the U.S. border. About $72 million in gross sales, for example, have been lost to the British Columbia dairy industry due to B.C. consumers purchasing cheap fluid milk and milk products south of the border.
Three of the five major crossings in B.C. have actually become known as milk and gas runs. Over 13,000 B.C. residents cross into Washington's border communities each day from B.C. often, I might add, for periods of less than half an hour basically just to fill up with gas, to purchase milk and dairy products, and then to return. I must point out that nobody can blame the residents of B.C. or anywhere across Canada for that matter, for trying to save a buck, particularly in a period of escalating gasoline prices and a weakening economy.
I would like to look at the consequences of what is happening with that haemorrhaging of money out of the provinces and down to the United States. In B.C. there is the loss of some $72 million is gross sales to British Columbia's dairy industry, some $30 million lost in provincial revenue from gasoline and transit taxes and $28 million lost in annual federal revenues. It can only be
called a haemorrhaging of dollars from our economy. It is kneecapping the British Columbia economy. It is helping to put people out of work.
This economic haemorrhage to the U.S. markets very clearly continues to grow, as the Canadian dollar has continued to be artifically elevated to accommodate the implementation of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. Canada's economy is still tied to an artificially strong dollar.
I might add that when one looks back from 1986 to 1989, the Canadian dollar rose 16 per cent against the U.S. dollar, making Canadian purchases of U.S. products increasingly attractive. This is the essence of the problem. What has resulted is an astounding 54 per cent increase in the number of Canadians travelling to the United States on same-day visits, presumably one would assume, to purchase cheaper U.S. goods. Of course, that would include dairy products.
I would like to point out that this correlation of a high Canadian dollar to this surging exodus of Canadian consumers is not coincidence. It is, I reiterate, an accelerating haemorrhage from our economy due to the fiscal policies of this government. It is hurting all economic sectors, particularly our dairy industry.
On June 27 I wrote to the minister again to press this issue further. The minister confirmed in his reply that studies done both in British Columbia and New Brunswick verify that up to 7.6 per cent of B.C. milk sales, and some 4.5 per cent of New Brunswick milk sales come from the United States. In other words, it is milk coming in from south of the border.
The recent attempt by the federal government to control this consumer import of dairy products, according to the dairy industry in B.C., has largely failed. Dairy farmers across Canada have asked the minister to consider the amendment of general import order No. 1, under the Export Import Control Act, to possibly include a provision for a minimum 48-hour stay or time allocation of some sort, so that one can use an import permit to control those dairy products coming across the border.
At the time of the original question in June, I asked the minister what steps he was prepared to take to curtail this loss to the economy in general, but in particular, to the dairy industry in British Columbia and elsewhere.

The minister at that time said that he was studying the situation and assured the House that once the data was gathered, he would sit down with the industry to consider an action plan. Five months have passed and I would like to know whether or not the study is completed and whether or not the minister and his associates have sat down with the dairy industry to work out a possible solution.
Does the minister have a solution to the problem at this time? I am not suggesting that we punish Canadian consumers by imposing stringent restraints. I am not suggesting that they be forced to endure large border line-ups by having customs officials process virtually every litre of milk that comes across the border into Canada. I am suggesting that we consider the provision of a time allocation for duty-free status and have a look at that option.
We should be looking at some mechanism to get the word out to Canadians throughout the provinces that every dollar that goes south of the border for U.S. purchase of milk, dairy products, gasoline and other products costs jobs in Canada. Essentially, it is a drain and a haemorrhaging of our national economy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the chance to discuss this government's concern over the purchase of U.S. dairy products by Canadian consumers.
Purchasers of dairy products are allowed if their value does not exceed $20 and are for personal use. In particular, they are allowed under general permit No. 1, issued by the Minister for International Trade. These imports are also subject to duty.
Adjournment Debate
Agriculture Canada has undertaken surveys in co-operation with customs and excise officials at border crossing points in British Columbia, New Brunswick and northern Ontario. The survey involves the use of statistical sampling techniques to estimate the extent of milk and cheese imports.
In 1988, at five border crossings in British Columbia, it was estimated that imports amounted to 7.6 per cent of fresh milk sales and 4.5 per cent of cheese sales. The survey also showed that retail prices of milk were from 36 to 60 per cent higher in British Columbia than in Washington state.
Retail prices for cheddar cheese were from 40 to 80 per cent higher on the Canadian side of the border. The results of that survey and a similar survey conducted in New Brunswick have both been published, and the results of a survey covering some border crossings in northern Ontario are also expected to be published by mid-November.
This issue has been raised on numerous occasions with dairy farmers, processors and retailers. When all the data is available, the Minister of Agriculture as well as the Minister for International Trade will sit down with the industry to see what steps can be taken to address this very serious issue.
However, I would like to point out that the regulation of fluid milk including pricing falls under provincial and not federal jurisdiction.
